title: Bintulu Marathon 2026 Review: Sarawak's Coastal-City 42K with AIMS Certification
seo_title: Bintulu Marathon 2026 Review | Sarawak Malaysia Race
meta_description: The Bintulu Marathon 2026: August 2 in Bintulu, Sarawak. AIMS-certified full marathon on Borneo's central coast — registration now closed.
dek: Set for 2 August 2026 at the Old Bintulu Airport site in Sarawak, this AIMS-certified full marathon has grown from 3,535 finishers in 2023 to a targeted 10,000 for 2026. Four distances with registration now closed.
verdict: The Bintulu Marathon has quietly become one of Malaysian Borneo's most significant road races. From its 2023 debut with 3,535 finishers, the event surged to 8,951 runners from 21 countries in 2025, with the Bintulu Development Authority targeting 10,000 for 2026 — a trajectory that reflects genuine organic demand. The 2026 edition carries AIMS and World Athletics international certification for the full and half marathon routes, a serious credential that puts Bintulu on the map for runners chasing internationally recognised times. The course crosses the Tun Taib Mahmud Bridge, offering views of Sungai Kuala Kemena that the BDA has described as breathtaking — and the kompang hand-drum group on the bridge adds Sarawak cultural texture that most city marathons would not think to provide. Four distances (42.195K with 7-hour cut-off, 21.1K with 4-hour cut-off, 10K, and 6K Fun Run) cover the full spectrum. The main watchout is the post-race litter issue that drew sharp criticism after 2025, with gel packets and cups scattered along the roadside despite bins at every water station; organisers face clear scrutiny to improve waste management. August in Sarawak is the southwest monsoon — warm and humid but generally drier than the November-to-February landas season. Registration is closed for 2026, but for anyone building a 2027 calendar, this is a flat, certified, growing Sarawak marathon worth the trip.

sections.heading: Bintulu: Sarawak's Central-Coast Industrial Hub
paragraphs: Bintulu sits roughly halfway between Kuching and Miri on Sarawak's central coast — a working port city built on oil, gas, and palm oil that has been methodically developing its sports-tourism infrastructure [1]. It is not a tourist town in the way Kuching is, but that is part of its appeal for runners seeking a genuine destination rather than a packaged experience: the town is flat, the roads are wide, and the BDA has put institutional weight behind building the marathon into a flagship event [1].

The start and finish at the Old Bintulu Airport site gives the race a dedicated, traffic-free precinct — a disused airstrip repurposed as an event hub with ample parking and assembly space [1]. The route across the Tun Taib Mahmud Bridge, while described by local press as challenging, rewards runners with open-water views of Sungai Kuala Kemena and the town skyline, and the kompang group stationed on the bridge delivers cultural energy that is uniquely Sarawakian [1].

sections.heading: From 3,535 to 10,000: The Growth Story
paragraphs: The Bintulu Marathon's growth curve is one of the more striking narratives in Malaysian road racing: 3,535 finishers in 2023, 5,800 in 2024, 8,951 from 21 countries in 2025, and a target of 10,000 for 2026 — nearly a threefold increase in three years [1]. Growth at that velocity would test any race organisation, but the BDA's institutional backing and the AIMS certification now attached to the routes signal that this is not a boom built on marketing alone.

International certification requires a standard of course measurement, timing infrastructure, and medical planning that separates serious marathons from community fun runs, and the BDA has invested in meeting those standards [1]. For runners chasing a Boston-qualifying time or simply wanting a certified result, the Bintulu Marathon now offers a legitimate credential on a predominantly flat coastal course.

sections.heading: The Course: Bridge Crossings and Coastal Flats
paragraphs: The 2026 full and half marathon routes are AIMS-certified, meaning they are measured to international standards and eligible for record-setting purposes [1]. The profile is predominantly flat — Bintulu sits on coastal floodplain — and the primary elevation challenge comes from bridge crossings rather than sustained climbs. The Tun Taib Mahmud Bridge section delivers the race's most memorable views, with Sungai Kuala Kemena stretching toward the South China Sea on one side and the town on the other.

Runners who tackled the 2025 edition in the rain — as one first-time half marathoner recounted online, describing the challenge of running in tropical downpour — should prepare for the possibility of wet conditions again [1]. August in Sarawak is the drier phase of the southwest monsoon, but equatorial Borneo does not respect statistical averages. The 7-hour and 4-hour cut-offs for the full and half respectively give mid-pack runners reasonable breathing room.

sections.heading: The Litter Issue: A Stain That Needs Addressing
paragraphs: The most significant blemish on the Bintulu Marathon's otherwise impressive trajectory is the post-race waste problem that drew criticism after 2025 [1]. Despite bins provided at every water station, used gel packets, disposable cups, and race detritus were left scattered along the roadside and across the bridge — a sight that local media described as marring what was otherwise an excellent turnout and smooth execution.

Local runners stepped up voluntarily to clean the course afterwards, with one participant publicly urging fellow runners to hold onto trash until reaching a bin [1]. For the 2026 edition, organisers face a clear test: improved bin placement, more assertive pre-race messaging, and a post-race cleanup crew deployed immediately behind the final wave. If the BDA wants Bintulu to be taken seriously as a regional destination race — and the AIMS certification says it does — the waste-management standard needs to match the operational standard.

sections.heading: Should You Run the Bintulu Marathon?
paragraphs: Registration for the 2 August 2026 edition is closed, so the practical question shifts to 2027. For runners building a multi-year calendar: Bintulu offers a flat, AIMS-certified course in an under-represented part of Malaysian Borneo, with four distance options, strong institutional backing, and a growth trajectory that suggests the event is being taken seriously [1]. The waste-management issue is real, but it is the kind of problem a maturing race organisation can solve with focused attention — and the BDA has both the resources and the reputational incentive to do so.

The destination case is stronger than it first appears: Bintulu is not Kuching, but it is a functional, affordable base from which to explore Sarawak's central coast, and the marathon weekend — with REPC at Boulevard Shopping Mall and a race-day start at the Old Bintulu Airport — is logistically straightforward. For runners who value certified courses, flat profiles, and the sense of being part of a race on an upward trajectory, the Bintulu Marathon belongs on the 2027 shortlist [1].

faqs.question: When is the Bintulu Marathon 2026 and where does it take place?
faqs.answer: The Bintulu Marathon 2026 takes place on 2 August 2026 in Bintulu, Sarawak, Malaysia. The race starts and finishes at the Old Bintulu Airport site, with Race Entry Pack Collection running from 30 July to 1 August 2026 at Boulevard Shopping Mall. Registration is now closed.

faqs.question: What distances are offered and what are the cut-off times?
faqs.answer: Four distances: full marathon (42.195 km, 7-hour cut-off), half marathon (21.1 km, 4-hour cut-off), 10 km (2h15m cut-off), and 6 km Fun Run (1h30m cut-off). Both the full and half marathon routes carry AIMS and World Athletics international certification for 2026.

faqs.question: Is the Bintulu Marathon course certified?
faqs.answer: Yes. The 2026 full and half marathon routes have received AIMS (Association of International Marathons and Distance Races) and World Athletics international certification, meaning they are measured to international standards and eligible for record-setting and qualifying purposes.

faqs.question: How fast has the Bintulu Marathon grown?
faqs.answer: The race has grown from 3,535 finishers in its 2023 debut, to 5,800 in 2024, to 8,951 runners from 21 countries in 2025. Organisers are targeting 10,000 participants for 2026 — nearly threefold growth in three years.

faqs.question: What was the litter issue after the 2025 race?
faqs.answer: After the 2025 edition, used energy gel packets and disposable cups were left scattered along the roadside and bridge despite bins at every water station. Local runners voluntarily cleaned the course afterwards. The organisers face scrutiny to improve waste management for 2026 with better bin placement, stronger pre-race messaging, and dedicated cleanup crews.
